 NEWMAN GROUP’S AND TEXAS SOUTHWEST COUNCIL-BOY SCOUTS OF AMERICA’S JOINT
              REPLY TO EXCEPTIONS TO PROPOSAL FOR DECISION

The intervenors, Newman Surface Properties, LP (NSP) and Cherokee Camp, LLC (Cherokee
Camp) (collectively the Newman Group) and Texas Southwest Council-Boy Scouts of America
(TSWC-BSA), timely file this Joint Reply to the Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision (PFD) in
the above-referenced cause in support of the Administrative Law Judges’ (ALJs’) recommendation
of Route 894 as the “best meets” route.

                                                    TABLE OF CONTENTS

                                                                                                                                        Page
I.     Introduction ......................................................................................................................... 2
II.    Legal Standard .................................................................................................................... 2

                   Newman Group’s and TSWC-BSA’s Joint Reply to the Exceptions to the PFD


    I.         INTRODUCTION

          1.     The Newman Group and TSWC-BSA file this Joint Reply to the Exceptions to the

PFD in support of the ALJ’s recommendation that Route 894 is the “best meets” route that meets

all applicable routing criteria under the Public Utility Regulatory Act (PURA) and the Public

Utility Commission’s (PUC’s) substantive rules. The Newman Group and TSWC-BSA take no

position on the issues of need and notice as considered in the PFD (i.e., Issues 1-7). The Newman

Group and TSWC-BSA agree that route 894 is the “best meets” route and the Commission should

decline to select Routes 295, 296, 572 and the Cherokee Creek RFI Route CCG (CCG) as the

“best meets” route.

          2.     The Commission must balance all the statutory and regulatory routing factors

without considering any one factor as determinative. The ALJs did just that and adequately

weighed the routing factors to recommend Route 894 as the “best meets” route in its extensive

PFD. The ALJs’ recommendation of Route 894 is further supported by all the routing factor

metrics, as outlined in the PFD. Additionally, the opposition groups to Route 894 rely on deficient

analyses to claim Route 894 is not the “best meets” route. As such, the Newman Group and

TSWC-BSA agree with the ALJs that Route 894 is the “best meets” route.


    II.        LEGAL STANDARD

          3.     The Commission must balance several routing factors when determining a specific

transmission line route, including the effects of the route on community values, recreation and park

areas, historic and aesthetic views, environmental integrity,1 engineering constraints, costs, grid




1 PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A)-(D).

reliability and security, whether routes will parallel or utilize existing electric facility rights of way

or other compatible rights of way (including highways, roads, railroads, or telephone utility rights

of way), whether routes parallel property lines or other natural or cultural features and whether

the routes conform with the policy of prudent avoidance.2

         4.        No one single routing factor is to receive greater weight or control.3 As such, the

Commission has the “authority to consider and weigh a variety of factors”4 delineated in PURA

§ 37.056 and 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.101(b)(3)(B)(i)-(iv). This is confirmed by Former Chairman

Smitherman’s testimony “that the route selection is ‘not a math question’ but rather a ‘balancing

of factors.’”5 The ALJs’ PFD sufficiently weighed these factors and applied them to four Focus

Routes (i.e. Issues 8-10) to recommend Route 894.6


    III.      THE PROPOSAL FOR DECISION ADEQUATELY BALANCED ROUTING FACTORS TO
              SELECT ROUTE 894 AS THE “BEST MEETS” ROUTE

         5.        The ALJs found Route 894 is the “best meets” as it is the "least bad option

available based on consideration of the routing factors.”7 In its exception to the PFD, Save the

Lampasas argues that Route 894 was chosen “on the basis of avoiding the Florence Elementary

School and limited analysis of any other routing factors.”8 Similarly, Cherokee Creek Aligned

Intervenors argue in their Exceptions to the PFD that the ALJ gave “insufficient weight to the full

range of criteria Texas law requires.”9 These arguments are misguided as the ALJs extensively

considered the routing factors from the Environmental Assessment (EA) and as outlined in PURA

§ 37.056(c) and in 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.101(b)(3)(B). The ALJs considered the following

routing factors in its PFD: community values, recreational and park areas, aesthetic and historic

values, environmental integrity, engineering constraints, route length and use of existing

compatible ROWs/property lines, cost, prudent avoidance and the impact to landowners.10

          6.      Specifically, the ALJs established that “every Focus Route has its advantages and

disadvantages,” and its analysis of the requisite factors supports the ALJ sufficiently weighed the

routing factors to land on Route 894.11 The PFD adequately weighed the factors without focusing

on any one specific factor. For example, the ALJs found Focus Routes 296 and 392 “perform

favorably on environmental considerations” but they have “considerable downsides.”12 Route 296

“runs within 500 feet of Florence Elementary School and two churches.”13 The ALJs additionally

determined Route 392 “has notably more habitable structures and cultural resources on it than

other Focus Routes.”14

          7.      The ALJs also held that routes “487 and 894 achieve prudent avoidance more

effectively than Routes 296 and 392”;15 however, between 487 and 894, Route 894 was declared

the better route.16 While 487 “has the highest percentage of parallelling compatible ROW,” it “also

has the largest impact on parks and recreation areas of the Focus Routes.” 17 Route 894 was

determined to be the best route as “no part of Route 894’s centerline runs within 1,000 feet of the

parks or recreational areas or is within the half-mile foreground visual zone of park and recreation

areas.”18 Further, the ALJs adequately weighed the required routing factors to determine Route

894 is the “best meets” route as “Route 894 performs favorably on habitable structures, paralleling

existing compatible ROW, crossing rangeland pasture, and crossing riparian areas.”19

           8.      The above analysis supports the ALJs adequately balanced the requisite factors to

ultimately find Route 894 the “best meets” route. No one factor was given greater weight, and all

advantages and disadvantages of the Focus Routes were considered.


     IV.         THE ALJ’S FINDING THAT ROUTE 894 IS THE “BEST MEETS” ROUTE IS
                 SUPPORTED BY THE ROUTING FACTOR METRICS

           9.      Route 894’s routing factor metrics support the ALJ’s selection as the “best meets”

route as opposed to the routes Newman Group and TXSWC-BSA oppose: Routes 295, 296, 572,

and CCG. Following the ALJs’ analysis of the PURA § 37.056(c)(4) factors, Route 894 outperforms

the above routes after all factors are weighed.

           10.     Habitable structures:20 Route 894 outperforms all Focus Routes and routes

295, 572, and CCG with respect to its impact on habitable structures. Route 894 has 85 habitable

has the least habitable structures within 500 feet of its centerline and does not run within 500 feet

of an elementary school.

        11.      Cost: While the ALJs “did not find cost to be a distinguishing factor in selecting a

route since the range of costs for the routes was in a relatively tight range,”23 Route 894 is less

expensive than all routes Newman Group and TXSWC-BSA oppose and is either cheaper or

comparable to the Focus Routes. Specifically, Route 894 will cost $1.681 billion, whereas Routes

295, 296, 572 and CCG cost $1.683 billion, $1.685 billion, $1.689 billion and $1.755 billion.24

        12.      Length: Route 894 is shorter in length than the routes Newman Group and

TXSWC-BSA oppose and is either shorter in length or comparable to the Focus Routes.25 Route

894 is 223.17 miles in length. 26 Routes 295, 296, 572, and CCG are 223.88, 223.78, 225.69, and

232.19 miles in length.27 Minimizing length further minimizes cost as a shorter route further

reduces construction and future maintenance costs as well.28

        13.      Recreation and Park Areas:29 Route 894 outperforms Routes 295 and 296 in

its impact to recreational and park areas as well. While Route 894 and the routes that Newman

Group and the TSWC-BSA opposes all have no parks or recreational areas within 1,000 feet of

each respective centerline, Route 894 performs better than routes 295 and 296 with respect to the

estimated length of right-of-way (ROW) within the foreground visual zone of park/rec areas. For

this metric, Route 894 is tied with Routes 572 and CCG at zero miles of ROW within the

foreground visual zone of park and recreational areas. 30 Routes 295 and 296 have an estimated

0.69 miles of ROW within the foreground visual zone of park/rec areas.31 No other filed route

compares to Route 894 in the concomitant minimization of habitable-structure impacts and zero

length of ROW within the foreground visual zone of park and recreation areas.32

        14.      Aesthetic and Historic Areas:33 Route 894 additionally minimizes impacts to

aesthetic and historic areas in comparison to Routes 295, 296, 572, and CCG. For example, Route

894 is tied with Route CCG for 2 recorded cultural resource sites crossed, while Routes 295 and

296 cross 4 recorded cultural resource sites and Route 572 crosses 3.34 Route 894 also has 12

recorded cultural resources within 1,000 feet of its centerline, where Routes 295 and 296 have 18,

Route 572 has 19, and Route CCG similarly has 18 within its centerline.35 Route 894 also

     V.          OPPOSITION GROUPS TO ROUTE 894 RELY ON DEFICIENT ANALYSES TO SUGGEST

                 894 IS NOT SUITABLE AS THE “BEST MEETS” ROUTE

          17.       The exceptions to the PFD filed by several groups that oppose the ALJs’

recommendation of Route 894 as the “best meets” route contain deficiencies. Staten Creek Ranch

argues the “Commission should place substantial weight on the qualitative impacts that this

proposed transmission line would have” on state parks as opposed to focusing on the “quantitative

performance of routes along the Central Corridor.”44 This analysis does not comport with the

requirement that all routing factors be balanced and no one factor be determinative. This

argument additionally puts undue and extra weight on qualitative factors such as aesthetic and

visual impacts. As noted above, no one factor should control the ultimate route selected for the

transmission line.45 It is also notable that Texas Parks & Wildlife did not participate nor comment

with any recommendations under Tex. Parks & Wildlife Code § 12.0011(b).46

          18.       Opposition groups to Route 894 also state that the ALJs conflated habitable

structures with “prudent avoidance.”47 The statutory definition of prudent avoidance is “[t[he

limiting of exposures to electric and magnetic fields that can be avoided with reasonable

investments of money and effort.48 A reduction in the amount of habitable structures within 500

feet of the centerline is precisely aligned with the requirement that the Commission consider

prudent avoidance. The ALJs contend that “limiting exposure to electric and magnetic fields can

be accomplished by choosing a route that has fewer habitable structures located near the route.”49

By minimizing the number of habitable structures near the route, exposure to electric and magnetic

fields are simultaneously limited. As such, the number of habitable structures near a route

centerline is intimately related to the requirement that the Commission consider prudent

avoidance in the selection of a route.

          19.    Carpenter Land and Cattle Co. claims path 296 can be “easily mitigated” to avoid

the Florence ISD Elementary School that is impacted by Link F34 on Route 296.50 This argument

fails to consider the inherent construction conflicts such a modification would entail.51 As noted in

Section IV above, Williamson County asserts that the county is undergoing construction projects

in which it has “already ‘invested substantial public resources’” into.52 Routes 295, 296, and 572

would substantially interfere with the County’s construction projects which are already part of the

County’s transportation plans.53 As stated in the Yates Keith Alliance and Williamson County

briefs, PUC Staff witness John Poole testified at the Hearing on the Merits that it would be “good

planning to try and avoid [this] transportation corridor” on State Highway 195 in Williamson

          20.     With respect to these reservations from different landowner groups, “the PUC is

expressly directed to consider the various factors and their impact on landowners to the extent

reasonable.”55 As such, while opposition groups have expressed various concerns regarding Route

894’s impacts to each landowner’s property, these considerations should be contemplated to an

extent but should not be determinative in the selection for the “best meets” route.


    VI.         CONCLUSION

          21.     The Newman Group and TSWC-BSA support the ALJs’ recommendation that

Route 894 is the “best meets” route. The ALJs sufficiently weighed the statutory and regulatory

routing factors to recommend Route 894 as the “best meets” route without reliance on any one

single factor. The routing factor metrics additionally support the ALJ’s recommendation of Route

894. The opposition groups to Route 894 further rely on flawed analyses to claim Route 894 is not

the “best meets” route in their exceptions to the PFD. As such, the Newman Group and TSWC-

BSA agree with the ALJs that Route 894 is the “best meets” route.
